name: Kedarnath Temple
deity: Shiva as Kedarnath, Lord of Kedara — the highest of the twelve Jyotirlingas
period: An ancient Himalayan shrine; tradition credits its revival to Adi Shankara in the 8th century
dynasty: Traditionally linked with the Pandavas and Adi Shankara
summary: High in the Garhwal Himalaya at the head of the Mandakini valley, Kedarnath is the loftiest of the twelve Jyotirlingas, first of the Panch Kedar and one of the Chota Char Dham — open only through the summer months.

sections.history: The Dvadasha Jyotirlinga Stotram honours "Kedara on the slopes of the Himalaya," and Kedarnath, at about 3,580 metres, is the highest of the twelve Jyotirlingas. Tradition holds that the Pandavas first built a shrine here and that Adi Shankara revived the temple in the 8th century; a memorial to the teacher stands behind it. Its worship is led by a Rawal, the chief priest, drawn by long custom from the Veerashaiva community of Karnataka. Kedarnath is also the first of the five Panch Kedar shrines and one of the four Chota Char Dham of Uttarakhand. In June 2013 flash floods swept through the valley, devastating the town and taking thousands of lives; the temple itself withstood the waters and has since welcomed pilgrims again.
sections.architecture: The temple is built of massive grey stone slabs set on a broad platform, its plain, sturdy walls and pyramidal roof made to endure Himalayan snow. A stone Nandi faces the entrance, and the pillared hall within is carved with images of the Pandavas, Kunti and Krishna. In the sanctum the linga is a natural, irregular rock, revered as the hump of Shiva in the form of a bull. Behind the temple rests a great boulder, the Bhim Shila, which lodged there in 2013 and turned the floodwaters aside.
sections.legends: After the Kurukshetra war, the Pandavas sought Shiva to be cleansed of the sin of killing their kin. Unwilling to meet them, Shiva hid among the herds of the Himalaya as a bull. Bhima recognised him, and as the bull sank into the ground he caught hold of its hump. That hump remained at Kedarnath, while, it is said, the arms appeared at Tungnath, the face at Rudranath, the navel at Madhyamaheshwar and the matted hair at Kalpeshwar — the five shrines of the Panch Kedar.
sections.festivals: The doors open each spring, around Akshaya Tritiya, on a date announced at Maha Shivaratri, and close on Bhai Dooj after Diwali. In winter the festival image is carried in a palanquin procession to the Omkareshwar temple at Ukhimath, where worship continues until the temple reopens. Shravan is a season of special devotion. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The last stretch to Kedarnath is made on foot, by pony or by helicopter, the path climbing beside the roaring Mandakini toward a ring of snow peaks. Arriving at the temple, with the white bulk of the Kedarnath range behind it, is for many the culmination of a lifetime's wish. Evening aarti in the thin, cold air is unforgettable; go slowly and allow time to acclimatise.

visit.timings: Open only from spring to early winter (roughly April–May to October–November); during the season darshan runs from early morning into the evening. Confirm opening and closing dates and daily timings locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest dress is expected, with warm layers essential at this altitude; footwear is removed before entering.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the temple; follow posted rules and staff guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Road access ends at Gaurikund (via Sonprayag) in Rudraprayag district, Uttarakhand, from where a steep trek of about 16–18 km leads to the temple; ponies, palanquins and helicopter services from the valley below are available. The nearest railway station is Rishikesh and the nearest airport is Jolly Grant, Dehradun. Pilgrim registration for the Char Dham yatra is required.
